catalog_quote: [p.71-72] Una is a language in which contrastive placement of pitch-accent carries a heavy functional load. The decision to consider Una a "pitch-accent language", instead of a word tone system with contrastive pitch on the accented syllable only, is due to the fact that each word has one and only one accent-carrying syllable which always carries a high pitch and has optionally more force. Monosyllabic words can be accented or unaccented. ... Polysyllabic words carry an accent on just one syllable which can be any syllable of the word. In Una the pitch of an unaccented syllable varies. But it is always lower than an emic high and it is about the same height as the following low. tone_statements.citation: Donohue, Mark. 2005. Tone and the Trans New Guinea languages. In Shigeki Kaji (ed.), Cross-linguistic studies of tonal phenomena: historical development, tone-syntax interface, and descriptive studies, 33-54. Tokyo: Research Institute for Languages and Cultures of Asia and Africa (ILCAA), Tokyo University of Foreign Studies.
tone_statements.quote: Examples of ‘prototypical’ pitch accent languages, with prelinking, no tone spreading and only one ‘melody’ can easily be found in the New Guinea region. Una is one example, and Arigibi Kiwai another. ... In Una, words of more than one syllable in length must bear an accent, but monosyllables are only optionally accented. In both cases there is no spreading of the tone unit associated with an accented syllable. ... Unlike Una, which REQUIRES at least one high pitched syllable in all but monosyllabic words, Kiwai has the restriction that at least one syllable per word must be low-pitched
tone_statements.locator: p.41, section 3, text above and below Table 2 'Pitch contrasts in Una.. and Arigibi Kiwai'
tone_statements.summary: Una = 'Pitch accent 1': one lexical accent (high pitch) per word, obligatory on polysyllables, optional on monosyllables (kal H 'tree sp.' vs kal L 'marsupial sp.'); no spreading. Second-hand data.

tone_statements.citation: Donohue, Mark. 1997. Tone systems in New Guinea. Linguistic Typology 1(3): 347-386. doi:10.1515/lity.1997.1.3.347
tone_statements.quote: [Una sh]ows an almost prototypical pitch-accent system (Louwerse 1978). Words of more than one syllable in Una must have one syllable which [is sp]oken at a higher pitch than the others; the difference between the [pat]tern of different words lies in the positioning of this pitch-accent. [Note] that the presence or absence of this accented syllable is not optional; [polys]yllabic words must contain one and only one accent.

tone_statements.summary: Every polysyllabic word has exactly one high-pitched accented syllable, monosyllables keep a two-way contrast, and words differ by where the accent sits. Matches the entry's Louwerse-based pitch accent description.

audit.reasoning: The tonal-OR-pitch accent coding rests on the dedicated primary phonology (Louwerse 1978, Irian 7(3):43-90), held as a page-image scan with scanned, and every deciding sentence was re-confirmed at pp.71-75 (author's explicit label 'pitch accent language'; one culminative high-pitch accent per word; placement contrastive and 'in most cases unpredictable'; two predictable subcases /-ɛb/ always accented, final [ə] never). The author's later reference grammar (PL B-100, 1988:9), also held, restates the same analysis and points back to 1978b. Glottolog 5.3 registers no other phonology or grammar for Una and no newer prosodic study was found, so the held source is the best available; the record's own note that lexical (free contrastive accent) would encode the same facts is accurate and is a labeling choice, not a sourcing gap.
